Apex Industrial Equipment Inc. - Q3 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Industrial Equipment Inc. Q3 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Apex Industrial Equipment Inc.'s results for the Q3 FY2024. Joining me on today's call are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Reynolds, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; and Dr. Emily Vargas, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Apex Industrial Equipment Inc.'s performance for the Q3. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. We saw robust order intake and favorable book-to-bill trends across end markets like construction, mining, and agriculture, which bolstered our backlog. Gross and operating margins continued to expand thanks to mix improvements and cost discipline. We're providing clear revenue guidance for Q4 and the full year, reflecting confidence in our trajectory. Lead times for key products and components have improved meaningfully, enhancing our competitiveness. Our dividend policy remains a key pillar, with a healthy yield supporting shareholder returns. Automation and digital offerings drove outsized growth while boosting efficiency for us and our customers. Overall book-to-bill ratios trended strongly, signaling backlog expansion. Even amid macroeconomic pressures, we've navigated end market demand effectively through strategic positioning.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Reynolds to provide more detail on our financial results.

Michael Reynolds (CFO):
Thank you, Johnathan. Turning to our financial performance, Apex Industrial Equipment Inc. reported $2.01 billion in revenue for the Q3, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 32.8%, driven by favorable product mix, pricing discipline, and supply chain leverage. Operating expenses were $425 million, resulting in an operating income of $285 million. Our net income for the quarter was $210 million, or $1.85 per share.

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call. As we dive into the details, I'd like to focus on our order intake and book-to-bill dynamics, which continue to underscore the strength and visibility in our $4.8 billion backlog—up 18% year-over-year and providing us with over 14 months of forward visibility at current production rates. Total order intake for the quarter came in at $3.2 billion, a robust 12% increase sequentially from Q2 and 22% higher year-over-year. This drove our consolidated book-to-bill ratio to 1.25x, well above our long-term target of 1.1x, reflecting healthy demand across our core end markets and our ability to convert that demand into a growing backlog.

Let me break this down by end market, where we saw differentiated performance tied to capex cycles, regional infrastructure tailwinds, and our strategic focus on electrification and autonomous systems. We'll reference our key product lines like the HX-series hydraulic excavators, TerraMax autonomous haul trucks, and PrecisionAg smart planters, which are gaining traction against peers like Caterpillar's 793F and John Deere's 8R tractors.

Construction remains our largest segment, with Q3 orders up 28% year-over-year and 15% sequentially. Book-to-bill here expanded to 1.35x from 1.18x a year ago, fueled by pent-up demand from the U.S. Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and Europe's NextGenerationEU recovery funds. In North America, which accounted for 55% of segment orders, we saw strong pull for our HX-450 excavators and compact track loaders, with intake surpassing $750 million—driven by data center builds and highway resurfacing projects. EMEA contributed 25%, benefiting from Germany's €100 billion special fund for infrastructure, though tempered by high interest rates delaying some municipal bids. APAC was softer at 15% of orders due to China's ongoing real estate slowdown, but we offset this with gains in India via our partnership with Larsen & Toubro on metro rail expansions. Strategically, our Gen4 electrification kits—retrofittable to 80% of our legacy fleet—secured $180 million in orders, positioning us ahead of Komatsu's electric mini-excavator ramp. We're on track to double electrified construction equipment sales to 25% of segment mix by FY2026. That's $1.35 billion in intake for construction, representing 42% of Q3 orders.

Mining orders grew 19% year-over-year and 8% sequentially, with a book-to-bill of 1.22x—supported by resilient commodity prices and operational leverage from Tier 1 producers. Copper and lithium demand, tied to the energy transition, drove 65% of intake, particularly our TerraMax autonomous haul trucks, which notched a record $420 million in bookings after successful pilots at BHP's Escondida mine in Chile. Iron ore remained steady, with Australian exposure via Rio Tinto contracts contributing 20%. LatAm, at 35% of mining orders, was a bright spot amid Brazil's Vale expansions, while North America dipped slightly due to paused capex at some U.S. gold operations. Challenges persist from labor shortages, but our AI-driven predictive maintenance via digital twins reduced downtime by 22% in customer fleets, boosting repeat orders. We're investing $250 million in a new Nevada battery plant to localize supply for electrified underground loaders, targeting 15% market share in battery-powered equipment by 2027—outpacing Sandvik's current ramp. Mining intake totaled $890 million, or 28% of Q3 orders.

Ag orders rose 14% year-over-year but were flat sequentially, yielding a book-to-bill of 1.10x amid weather headwinds in the U.S. Midwest and Brazil's delayed planting season. PrecisionAg products, like our AI-optimized planters and autonomous sprayers, drove 40% of intake at $230 million, with strong adoption from large-scale operators like Archer Daniels Midland. North America led at 48%, buoyed by farm income resilience and USDA subsidies, while Brazil's 25% share reflected soybean recovery post-drought. EMEA grew 12% on EU CAP reforms favoring sustainable tech, but APAC lagged due to rural financing constraints in India. Our strategic edge here is the AgroLink telematics platform, now integrated with John Deere Operations Center APIs, which improved yield mapping accuracy by 18% in beta trials—securing OEM co-development deals worth $100 million in future backlog. We're guiding for ag book-to-bill to inflect to 1.20x in FY2025 as harvest cycles normalize and our electric tractor line launches. Ag intake was $575 million, 18% of orders.

This bucket including oil & gas and forestry posted 25% YOY growth with a 1.40x book-to-bill. LNG-related rig upgrades in the Permian and Qatar drove energy equipment orders, while sustainable forestry harvesters gained in Canada amid ESG mandates. Other intake $385 million, 12% of orders.

North America (52% of total orders) was the growth engine at +26% YOY, leveraging IIJA and reshoring trends. EMEA (22%) grew 16%, offset by energy costs but lifted by green deals. APAC (16%) was +9%, with India and Southeast Asia compensating for China. LatAm (10%) surged 32% on mining and ag rebounds.

These trends affirm our 'Tech-Forward Industrials' strategy: 35% of Q3 orders were for next-gen products (electrified, autonomous, connected), up from 22% last year, driving 400bps of gross margin expansion. We're expanding capacity 20% at our Peoria excavator plant and Monterrey mining fab, funded by $1.2 billion in free cash flow. Risks include geopolitical tensions in LatAm and potential U.S. Fed cuts delaying capex, but our backlog derisking and 65% aftermarket exposure provide stability. We expect Q4 order intake of $3.3-3.5 billion, with book-to-bill sustained above 1.2x, positioning us for mid-teens EPS growth in FY2025.

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for Apex Industrial Equipment Inc., or Apex as many of you know us. Today, I'd like to dive deep into our gross margin and operating margin trends, which continue to reflect the strength of our strategic execution amid a dynamic industrial landscape. As a leader in precision CNC machining centers, hydraulic systems for heavy equipment, and automation solutions for factory floors, we've navigated headwinds like volatile commodity inputs and softening demand in select end-markets while capitalizing on tailwinds from reshoring and electrification megatrends.

Gross margins came in at 32.8% for Q3, up 210 basis points year-over-year and 50 basis points sequentially from Q2's 32.3%. This marks our third consecutive quarter of expansion, bringing our trailing 12-month gross margin to 31.9%, a 320 basis point improvement from the prior-year period. For context, this outperforms the broader industrial equipment peer set—think Caterpillar's recent 30% range or Ingersoll Rand's mid-30s—positioning us at the higher end of the spectrum.

Driving this expansion were several key factors, deeply rooted in our industry dynamics: Favorable product mix and pricing discipline: Approximately 45% of our Q3 revenue came from higher-margin automation and digitalization products, including our next-gen RoboForge robotic welding systems and AI-enabled predictive maintenance kits for CNC mills. These segments delivered gross margins north of 38%, up from 35% a year ago, as customers prioritize Industry 4.0 upgrades amid labor shortages. Average selling prices, or ASPs, rose 4.2% YoY, supported by our dynamic pricing model that adjusts for steel and aluminum surcharges—critical given LME copper prices spiking 15% in the quarter.

Supply chain resilience and COGS leverage: Raw material costs, which comprise 55% of our COGS, moderated as global steel prices eased 8% from their Q1 peaks, thanks to destocking in China and improved U.S. mill utilization. We locked in 70% of our 2024 steel needs via long-term contracts at $850/ton, below spot rates, while our vertical integration in hydraulic component forging—now at 65% insourcing—shaved 150 basis points off variable costs. Capacity utilization hit 88% across our 12 global plants, up from 82% last year, generating meaningful absorption of fixed manufacturing overheads.

Regionally, North America was the star, contributing 55% of revenue with gross margins at 34.2%, fueled by onshoring in semiconductors and EVs—our hydraulic presses for battery gigafactories saw 25% volume growth. Europe lagged at 29.5% margins due to energy surcharges from the Ukraine conflict, but we're mitigating via localized sourcing from Turkey and Poland. APAC margins held steady at 31%, with strength in India's infrastructure boom offsetting softness in China's property sector.

That said, we're not complacent. Freight and labor inflation added 40 basis points of pressure in Q3, reminiscent of 2022's supply disruptions. Our technical initiatives—like deploying digital twins for supply chain simulation across our ERP system and piloting generative AI for demand forecasting—have reduced inventory days from 95 to 82, unlocking $150 million in working capital and indirectly bolstering margins.

Turning to operating margins, which expanded to 14.2% in Q3—up 180 basis points YoY and 30 basis points sequentially—our operating income reached $285 million on $2.01 billion of revenue. Trailing 12-month op margin now stands at 13.8%, approaching our long-term target of 15% by FY2025.

This leverage stems from disciplined OpEx management: SG&A efficiency: Held flat at 12.1% of revenue versus 12.8% last year, despite $20 million in incremental sales force investments for our electrification platform. We achieved this through zero-based budgeting and offshore-ing back-office functions to our Manila shared services center, cutting admin costs 9%.

R&D productivity: R&D spend rose modestly to 4.2% of revenue, focused on high-ROI projects like our e-Hydro electric actuator line for wind turbine nacelles—already securing $500 million in orders from Vestas and Siemens Gamesa. This mix shift drove a 25% ROIC uplift in new product revenue, which now comprises 28% of total sales.

Regional nuance: U.S. ops delivered 15.8% margins on strong aftermarket parts sales (up 12% YoY), while EMEA's 11.5% reflected restructuring charges from idling a legacy plant in Germany. Asia-Pacific ops margins hit 14.5%, benefiting from our ASEAN assembly hubs serving EV supply chains.

Strategically, these trends validate our 'Margin First' playbook: accelerating premium mix to 50% by 2026 via acquisitions like our recent $400 million tuck-in of a U.S. precision robotics firm; advancing lean sigma programs targeting another 200 basis points of gross margin by optimizing our 85% automated lines; and hedging 60% of FX exposure amid a strong USD pressuring exports.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 gross margins of 33.0-33.5%, with op margins of 14.5-15.0%, assuming stable commodity inputs and 5-7% organic revenue growth. Risks include potential steel tariffs or a deeper Eurozone slowdown, but our $1.2 billion cash pile and 2.1x net debt-to-EBITDA provide ample dry powder.

Thank you, Johnathan. Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us on the call. Before I dive into the details of our Q4 and full-year revenue guidance, let me quickly recap our Q3 performance, which sets the stage here. We delivered Q3 revenue of $2.01 billion, up 12% year-over-year and 5% sequentially, driven primarily by a 18% surge in our Automation and Robotics segment—think our next-gen collaborative robots and AI-integrated CNC machining centers, which are seeing strong uptake in automotive EV production lines. Aftermarket services also grew 14%, benefiting from higher machine utilization rates amid the ongoing reshoring wave in North America.

Now, turning to guidance. For the fourth quarter, we are guiding revenue to $2.08 billion to $2.14 billion. That's a year-over-year growth range of 10% to 13%, and roughly flat to up 6% sequentially from Q3. Let me break this down by key drivers and regions to give you the full picture.

First, segment trends: We expect our core Equipment segment—which includes our heavy-duty stamping presses, precision lathes, and hydraulic forming systems—to contribute about 55% of Q4 mix, growing mid-single digits year-over-year. This reflects sustained demand from aerospace and defense, where we're fulfilling multi-year backlog from programs akin to Boeing's 737 MAX ramp-up and Lockheed Martin's F-35 sustainment. Automation and Robotics should accelerate to 20%+ growth, fueled by our new ApexFlex platform, which integrates edge AI for predictive maintenance—early wins include deployments at Tesla's Gigafactory Texas and Stellantis' Windsor assembly plant. Services and Parts, at around 25% of mix, remain our high-margin bedrock, with growth in the low teens as fleet utilization hits 85%, up from 78% a year ago.

Regionally, North America will be our growth engine at 15% year-over-year, representing over 50% of Q4 revenue. CHIPS Act funding and IRA incentives are accelerating fab construction—think Intel's Ohio greenfield and TSMC's Arizona site—driving orders for our semiconductor wafer handling equipment and cleanroom robotics. EMEA, however, tempers the outlook with flat to low-single-digit growth due to lingering energy headwinds in Germany and softening machinery capex in autos post-Volkswagen's ID.4 production adjustments. Asia-Pacific should deliver high-single-digit growth, led by China's EV battery push—we're seeing pull-ins for lithium-ion cell formers similar to CATL's expansions—and India's PLI scheme boosting orders from Tata and Mahindra for ag-industrial tractors.

A few strategic insights worth highlighting: Supply chain resilience is paying off. Our dual-sourcing strategy for critical components like rare-earth magnets and precision actuators has de-risked us from prior disruptions, with lead times now down to 12 weeks from 24. On the technical front, we're ramping our Industry 4.0 initiatives—over 40% of Q4 bookings will feature IoT connectivity via our ApexCloud platform, enabling real-time OEE optimization and reducing downtime by up to 25% for customers. Sustainability is another tailwind; our electric hydraulic presses, with 30% lower energy draw than legacy pneumatics, are qualifying for EU CBAM credits and U.S. green procurement lists.

For the full fiscal year 2024, we now guide revenue to $8.0 billion to $8.2 billion, implying 11% to 13% growth over FY2023's $7.2 billion. This raises our prior guide by $150 million at the midpoint, reflecting better-than-expected book-to-bill of 1.15x and backlog growth to $4.8 billion, up 22% year-over-year. Margins should expand accordingly, with adjusted EBITDA at 18% to 19% of revenue, supported by operating leverage and pricing actions averaging 4% across the portfolio.

Looking ahead to FY2025, early indicators are constructive: RFIs for U.S. infrastructure via the IIJA are converting at 70% rates for our bridge fabrication gear, and generative AI hype is spilling into factory floor pilots—our Rockwell-compatible PLC upgrades are in trials at Foxconn. That said, we're mindful of macro risks like potential softening in non-residential construction and FX headwinds from a stronger USD.

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for Apex Industrial Equipment. As we dive into the operational metrics that are driving our record backlog of $4.8 billion—up 18% year-over-year—let's turn to one of the most critical levers in our business: lead times for our key products and components. In the industrial equipment sector, where customers like those in mining, oil & gas, and heavy construction demand reliability and speed, lead times directly correlate to book-to-bill ratios, customer retention, and our ability to capture pricing premiums amid persistent inflation in raw materials.

To set the stage, our company-wide average lead time for core products—think our flagship hydraulic excavators, high-pressure pumps, and CNC machining centers—stood at 14.2 weeks at quarter-end, a robust 22% improvement from 18.1 weeks in Q3 last year and a sequential 8% reduction from Q2's 15.4 weeks. This puts us ahead of industry peers; for context, Caterpillar reported excavator lead times around 20 weeks in their last update, while our book-to-bill of 1.35x reflects the pull from hyperscalers and OEMs restocking after the 2023 supply chain normalization.

Breaking it down by product line, our excavator portfolio—accounting for 28% of Q3 revenue—saw lead times compress to 12 weeks from 19 weeks YoY, thanks to ramped capacity at our Peoria, Illinois facility, where we've idled a third assembly line at 95% utilization. High-pressure pumps for fracking and water management, which represent 15% of sales, improved to 11.5 weeks, down from 16 weeks, driven by dual-sourcing forged steel components from U.S. mills like Nucor amid Section 232 tariff stability. On the flip side, our precision CNC lathes for aerospace OEMs like Boeing and Spirit AeroSystems held steady at 16 weeks, as titanium alloy shortages persist—global spot prices up 12% QoQ per S&P Global data—but we've mitigated this with forward contracts covering 70% of 2024 needs.

Shifting to components, which feed 60% of our backlog, lead times here are even more telling of our supply chain resilience. Critical castings and forgings—like those A36 steel housings for our gear reducers—dropped to 5.8 weeks from 9.2 weeks YoY, a 37% improvement, after implementing vendor-managed inventory (VMI) programs with key suppliers such as ArcelorMittal. Electronic controls and PLCs, however, remain a pain point at 7.9 weeks, pressured by the ongoing semiconductor cycle; despite TSMC's Fab 21 ramp-up in Arizona, lead times for automotive-grade MCUs from Infineon are still 12-14 weeks industry-wide. We've de-risked this by qualifying domestic alternatives from Microchip Technology, reducing exposure by 40% since Q1.

Regionally, the picture varies significantly, underscoring our strategic footprint. In North America, which drove 52% of Q3 orders, average lead times are a crisp 12.8 weeks—best-in-class—bolstered by the CHIPS Act subsidies accelerating onshoring. Our Fort Worth plant is now shipping 85% of U.S. hydraulic cylinders within 10 weeks, capitalizing on the shale boom where E&Ps like ExxonMobil are front-loading CapEx. Europe, at 42% of revenue, lags at 16.5 weeks due to energy transition headwinds; wind turbine OEMs like Vestas are delaying orders amid Red Sea disruptions adding 3-4 weeks to Baltic shipping routes, but our Hamburg warehouse—stocked with 20,000 tons of Euro 7-compliant components—has trimmed this by 15% via just-in-time (JIT) kanban with local fabricators.

Asia-Pacific, our growth engine at 6% of sales but 12% order growth, faces the longest tails at 18.2 weeks, fueled by a semiconductor fab expansion frenzy—think TSMC's Japan plants and Samsung's Texas moves indirectly straining regional logistics. China tariffs and Typhoon Gaemi disruptions pushed container rates up 25% MoM per Drewry Index, but our new Suzhou JV with a Howa Machinery partner has localized 30% of gearbox production, targeting sub-15-week delivery by year-end.

What’s behind this progress? We've invested $180 million YTD in technical initiatives that are paying off handsomely. First, our Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) upgrade to SAP S/4HANA with AI-driven demand sensing has improved forecast accuracy to 92%, cutting excess inventory by 22% while filling backlog holes proactively—similar to Honeywell's playbook in industrial IoT. Second, digital twin simulations via Siemens NX software at our six global plants have optimized production sequencing, shaving 1.2 weeks off machining cycles for complex assemblies like our variable-frequency drives (VFDs). Third, we're piloting advanced manufacturing with fiber-laser additive processes for turbine blades, reducing forging lead times by 45% in prototypes; scaling this could mirror GE Vernova's HA turbine efficiencies.

Strategically, these shorter lead times are unlocking margin expansion. Customers are willing to pay a 5-7% premium for sub-12-week delivery on high-margin products like our 500-ton presses, boosting ASPs 4% QoQ. We're also converting 25% more spot orders into frame agreements, echoing Deere & Company's ag equipment surge during the 2022 commodity cycle. Capacity-wise, we're at 88% utilization enterprise-wide, with $250 million earmarked for 2025 CapEx to add 15% throughput—prioritizing nearshoring in Mexico via our Monterrey expansion to hedge U.S.-China tensions.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 lead times to stabilize at 13.5-14.5 weeks, assuming no major port strikes or steel price spikes above $800/ton CFR. Upside risks include IIJA-funded infrastructure pours accelerating pump demand, while downside from a China slowdown could ease component pressures. Our visibility remains strong with a $4.8 billion backlog entering 2025, positioning us to outperform in a market where peers like Komatsu are still quoting 22+ weeks on dozers.

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for Apex Industrial Equipment, where we're reporting another solid quarter in the industrial machinery sector, with adjusted EPS of $1.85, up 12% year-over-year, driven by robust demand for our precision CNC machining centers and automated material handling systems amid the ongoing reshoring of U.S. manufacturing.

Now, turning to our dividend policy and yield, which remains a cornerstone of our capital allocation strategy as a mature leader in the industrial equipment space—much like our peers at Caterpillar and Ingersoll Rand. We view consistent, growing dividends not just as a return to shareholders, but as a disciplined signal of our confidence in the long-term secular tailwinds reshaping our industry: Industry 4.0 digitization, the electrification of heavy machinery, and supply chain localization post-COVID disruptions.

Let's start with the numbers. Today, our Board approved a quarterly dividend of $0.62 per share, payable on December 15th to shareholders of record as of November 25th. This marks a 9% increase over last quarter's $0.57 and continues our streak of 28 consecutive years of dividend growth—placing us in elite company alongside Cummins and Deere, who've navigated multiple cycles from the 2008 financial crisis to the 2022 supply chain crunch.

Annualized, this equates to $2.48 per share, delivering a current forward yield of 2.4% based on yesterday's closing price of $103.25. For context, that's competitive within our peer group: Caterpillar's at 1.6%, while Ingersoll Rand sits around 0.8%, reflecting our more balanced payout versus aggressive growth reinvestment. Our trailing 12-month yield stands at 2.3%, up from 1.9% a year ago, benefiting from a 15% stock appreciation tied to our outperformance in aftermarket services, which now comprise 42% of revenue—think predictive maintenance IoT kits for our legacy hydraulic press lines.

Our policy is straightforward yet flexible: target a 40-50% payout ratio of adjusted free cash flow, ensuring we prioritize sustainable growth over short-term spikes. In Q3, we generated $285 million in adjusted FCF, up 18% YoY, thanks to working capital efficiencies from our new ERP implementation across our North American forging plants. This covered our $112 million dividend payout (39% ratio) while leaving ample room for $150 million in capex—focused on retrofitting our assembly lines with collaborative robots (cobots) from partners like Universal Robots—and $75 million in share repurchases under our $500 million authorization, now 60% complete.

Strategically, this discipline shines in the current environment. Regionally, North America remains our dividend fortress, contributing 55% of FCF from infrastructure spend under the IIJA, where our road milling equipment is seeing 25% order growth. Asia-Pacific, at 28% of revenue, is accelerating with India's PLI scheme boosting demand for our electric arc furnace controls—yields here are enhanced by lower regional capex intensity. Europe, however, tempers optimism: energy costs from the Ukraine crisis have pushed our payout conservatism, with German auto OEMs delaying capex on stamping presses, capping EMEA at 17% of FCF.

Looking ahead, we're committed to 8-10% annual dividend growth through the cycle, supported by our $4.8 billion order backlog (up 14% YoY) and margin expansion from technical initiatives like AI-driven yield optimization in our additive manufacturing division—piloting with Boeing for titanium aerospace components, targeting a 200 bps gross margin lift to 32% by FY25. We've stress-tested this against headwinds: even in a mild recession with industrial production flatlining like Q1 2023, our FCF coverage exceeds 2.2x dividends, bolstered by our 65% localization rate in U.S. supply chains, mitigating tariff risks on imported steel castings.

In short, our dividend isn't static—it's dynamic, balancing shareholder returns with the $400 million R&D pipeline for next-gen sustainable equipment, like hydrogen-ready turbine housings amid the energy transition. We believe this positions Apex to outperform the S&P Industrials average yield of 1.7%, delivering total returns north of 10% annually.

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us on Apex Industrial Equipment's third quarter earnings call. As we dive into our segment performance, I'd like to spend some time on one of our fastest-growing areas: our automation and digital offerings portfolio. This segment, which now represents 18% of our total revenue—up from just 12% a year ago—delivered exceptional results this quarter, growing 32% year-over-year and 11% sequentially. That's ahead of our guided 25-30% full-year growth target, driven by surging demand for Industry 4.0 solutions amid global manufacturing reshoring and the push for operational resilience.

Let me break this down with some specifics. Our core automation revenue, including robotic systems like our next-gen AutoArm 5000 series—comparable to Fanuc's CRX collaborative robots but optimized for heavy industrial environments—grew 28% YoY to $245 million. These systems are seeing strong uptake in automotive and semiconductor fab applications, where cycle times have improved by an average of 22% for our customers, based on post-installation audits. But the real story is in our digital offerings, which exploded 45% YoY to $180 million. This includes our flagship DigiForge platform, a cloud-edge hybrid suite that integrates IIoT sensors, AI-powered predictive analytics, and digital twins—much like Siemens' MindSphere but tailored for discrete manufacturing with sub-millisecond latency via 5G edge computing.

On efficiency impacts, these offerings are transforming our customers' P&Ls in ways that create sticky, high-margin recurring revenue for us. Take overall equipment effectiveness, or OEE: Across our installed base of over 15,000 connected assets, we're delivering an average 15-20% uplift. For instance, in a recent deployment at a major Tier-1 EV battery producer in the U.S. Midwest—think something akin to Panasonic's Kansas Gigafactory—our anomaly detection algorithms, powered by machine learning models trained on petabytes of vibration, thermal, and torque data, reduced unplanned downtime by 35%. That translated to $12 million in annual savings for them, with energy consumption dropping 18% through optimized servo motor controls. Marginally, our digital services now carry 72% gross margins, versus 42% for traditional hardware, pulling our segment EBITDA margin to 31%—up 450 basis points YoY.

Regionally, the trends are telling. In North America, which accounted for 42% of segment sales, growth was 38% YoY, fueled by reshoring initiatives under the CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act. We're seeing hyperscalers like TSMC's Arizona fabs adopting our wafer fab automation stacks, where throughput yields have jumped 12% via real-time process orchestration. EMEA delivered 29% growth, driven by EU Green Deal mandates; our energy-efficient digital twins helped a German steel mill—similar to ThyssenKrupp—cut Scope 1 emissions by 22% while boosting yield by 8%. Asia-Pacific was our star at 40% growth, with China’s 'Made in China 2025' policy accelerating robot density to over 400 per 10,000 workers. Partnerships with local OEMs like SANY have embedded our AutoLink IIoT modules into crane and CNC systems, capturing 15% market share in that sub-segment.

Strategically, we're leaning into servitization harder than ever. Over 60% of our new automation deals now include as-a-service contracts—think 'Robotics-as-a-Service' with uptime SLAs backed by our global NOC (Network Operations Center). This has driven ARR from digital subscriptions to $320 million, up 55% YoY, with net retention rates hitting 128%. We've invested $150 million in R&D this year, including a collaboration with NVIDIA for GPU-accelerated edge AI, enabling over-the-air firmware updates that adapt to supply chain volatility in real-time. Looking ahead, we see this segment compounding at 30%+ CAGR through 2027, outpacing the broader industrial automation market's 12% trajectory per IDC forecasts. Risks like semiconductor lead times persist, but our diversified supply chain—40% domestic sourcing now—mitigates that.

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call. Today, I'd like to dive into our book-to-bill dynamics, which continue to be a strong leading indicator of our growth trajectory in the industrial equipment sector. For those less familiar, the book-to-bill ratio is calculated as our quarterly bookings—new orders secured—divided by our billings, which represent revenue recognized from shipments and services. A ratio above 1.0 signals backlog expansion and future revenue visibility, which is critical in our capital-intensive industry where lead times for complex systems like CNC machining centers, robotic automation lines, and heavy-duty material handling equipment can stretch 6 to 12 months.

In Q3, we delivered a book-to-bill of 1.25x, up from 1.18x in Q2 and markedly ahead of the 1.05x we posted in Q3 of last year. This marks our strongest quarterly reading since Q4 2021, during the post-pandemic capex rebound. On a trailing 12-month basis, our ratio stands at 1.22x, reflecting sustained demand momentum. This performance drove a 17% year-over-year increase in our ending backlog to $4.8 billion, providing exceptional visibility into FY24 and well into FY25—about 1.4x our expected annual revenue run rate.

Breaking it down by segment, our Automation & Robotics division led the way with a robust 1.42x book-to-bill, fueled by hyperscaler investments in semiconductor fab expansions and EV battery gigafactories. Orders here surged 28% YoY, including major wins for our next-gen collaborative robot arms integrated with AI-driven vision systems, similar to what we've seen at peers like Fanuc and ABB. Discrete Manufacturing came in at 1.15x, benefiting from reshoring tailwinds in North American aerospace and defense—think Boeing and Lockheed ramp-ups—while our Process Equipment segment, which includes pumps and valves for oil & gas and chemicals, held steady at 1.08x amid volatile energy markets.

Regionally, the story is equally compelling. North America was the standout at 1.35x, up 200 basis points sequentially, driven by the Inflation Reduction Act's incentives for domestic manufacturing.
